title: A EUR 60,000 payment from Europe to India took four days, and neither side could say where it was
explain:
A European buyer paid an Indian exporter EUR 60,000.

The payment travelled through a chain of correspondents and took four days.

Neither side could say where it was on any of those days.

Here's how it happened:

→ European buyer sends EUR 60,000 to an Indian exporter
→ Payment passes through a chain of correspondents
→ Each hop adds a day and a fee
→ No single party can track the payment end to end
→ Exporter waits, buyer cannot confirm delivery

The assumption was:
"A chain of correspondents is a payment corridor."

Why?

It is not. A corridor without a trackable path is just a longer chain of correspondents. Building a payment corridor from India to Europe means mapping every dependency: currency, scheme, compliance, data, FX and settlement, and replacing that chain with a defined path that both sides can track.

A chain is not a corridor.

BA Takeaway

A bridge design must replace the correspondent chain with a defined, trackable path. If neither side can track the payment, the bridge does not exist yet.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Currency and FX
→ Scheme and compliance
→ Data and settlement
→ The trackable path, visible to both sides

The real requirement isn't "Can the payment reach India?"

It's "What evidence proves both sides can track it at every step?"

Have you seen a cross-border payment disappear into a correspondent chain for days?
takeaway: A chain is not a corridor.

title: Zero-fee weekend: volume hits 300 percent of peak
explain:
A bank launches a zero-fee weekend campaign for retail payments.
Within the first hour payment volume rises to 300 percent of a normal peak, three times the usual load.
Latency climbs, channel sessions start timing out, and the clearing connector queue grows faster than it drains.

Here's how that happens:

→ Campaign launches, zero fees
→ Volume rises to 300 percent of a normal peak
→ Latency climbs and sessions time out
→ Clearing queue grows faster than it drains

The assumption was:
"The system handled last year's peak, so it will handle the campaign."

Averages hide the risk, and this surge is not an average day. Treat the surge as a capacity problem with three controls: intake, queue and recovery. At intake, apply back-pressure through the API gateway and channel, queue or gracefully defer non-critical traffic, show a clear pending state instead of a silent timeout, and throttle campaign traffic to a rate the downstream chain can sustain.

Averages hide peaks. Peaks break systems.

BA Takeaway

Control the surge at intake before it reaches the clearing connector. Back-pressure, graceful deferral and a clear pending state beat a silent timeout, and campaign traffic is throttled to a rate the downstream chain can sustain.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Intake and back-pressure
→ Queue depth
→ Recovery and retry

The real requirement isn't "How much volume did we get?"

It's "What evidence proves the peak fits inside measured capacity?"

Have you ever watched a campaign triple the load in an hour and the queue grow faster than it drained?
takeaway: At intake, apply back-pressure, queue or gracefully defer non-critical traffic, show a clear pending state instead of a silent timeout, and throttle campaign traffic to a rate the downstream chain can sustain.

title: Two banks, no account between them, EUR 40,000 still arrives
explain:
A customer wants to transfer EUR 40,000 to a bank that holds no account with the sending bank.
There is no direct relationship, no nostro, no vostro.
The payment still arrives.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sending bank has no account with the beneficiary bank
→ Sending bank passes the instruction to its correspondent
→ Correspondent passes it onward
→ Payment reaches the beneficiary bank

The assumption was:
"No direct account means no payment."

A customer can transfer funds to a bank that has no account with the sending bank, because the payment travels through correspondent and intermediary banks that do hold accounts with each other. The sending bank passes the instruction to its correspondent, which passes it onward until it reaches a bank that holds an account for the beneficiary bank. The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship.

The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship.

BA Takeaway

Follow the chain, not the direct link. Each correspondent passes the instruction to the next bank that holds an account, until the chain reaches a bank that holds an account for the beneficiary bank.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sending bank
→ Correspondent bank
→ Next correspondent in the chain
→ Beneficiary bank

The real requirement isn't "Do we hold an account with them?"

It's "What evidence proves the chain reaches a bank that holds their account?"

Have you ever traced a payment through three correspondents to reach a bank your bank had never dealt with?
takeaway: The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship.

title: The sterling leg went through CHAPS. The payment still had to leave the UK.
explain:
A cross-border payment needs sterling settlement in the UK, so the team routes the domestic leg through CHAPS.
The CHAPS leg settles cleanly in central bank money.
Then the payment stops, because nobody arranged the leg out of the UK, and the GBP 120,000 sits in London.

Here's how that happens:

→ Cross-border payment needs sterling settlement
→ CHAPS settles the domestic sterling leg
→ No correspondent or scheme arranged for the leg out of the UK

The assumption was:
"CHAPS can carry a payment abroad."

CHAPS settles sterling payments between UK banks in central bank money, and a cross-border payment that needs sterling settlement in the UK can use it as the domestic leg. The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey.

CHAPS settles sterling at home. The cross-border leg still needs a correspondent.

BA Takeaway

Plan both legs. CHAPS is the domestic sterling leg, settled in central bank money, and the leg out of the UK needs a correspondent or a scheme of its own.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic sterling leg, CHAPS
→ Cross-border leg, correspondent or scheme
→ Settlement in central bank money

The real requirement isn't "Did the CHAPS leg settle?"

It's "What evidence proves the leg out of the UK is arranged?"

Have you ever settled the domestic leg perfectly and forgotten the payment still had to leave the country?
takeaway: The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey.

title: GBP 10,000 crossed borders with no SWIFT message at all
explain:
A customer sends GBP 10,000 to a beneficiary abroad.
No SWIFT message is sent for either leg.
The beneficiary is paid, on time, and the sending bank never touched the correspondent chain.

Here's how that happens:

→ Customer funds a local account in the sending country
→ Provider pays the beneficiary from its local account abroad
→ Each leg settles domestically
→ Flows netted across customers

The assumption was:
"Every cross-border payment needs SWIFT."

The provider holds local accounts in the countries it serves and settles each leg domestically. A customer paying from one country to another funds a local account in the sending country, and the provider pays the beneficiary from its local account in the receiving country, so no cross-border SWIFT message is needed for the legs. The model works because the provider nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain.

Two domestic legs can replace one cross-border chain.

BA Takeaway

Recognise the design for what it is. Local funding in, local payout out, flows netted across customers, and no SWIFT message on either leg. It is not correspondent banking done badly. It is a different model.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Local funding leg
→ Local payout leg
→ Netting across customers
→ No SWIFT leg

The real requirement isn't "Where is the SWIFT message?"

It's "What evidence proves each leg settled, and who holds the funds in between?"

Have you ever looked for a SWIFT message that was never sent, because the payment never crossed a border as a message?
takeaway: The model works because the provider nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain.

title: The beneficiary bank has a BIC that cannot receive messages
explain:
A EUR 65,000 payment is addressed to a bank whose BIC has the digit 1 in position 8.
That marks it as non-connected: a SWIFT participant that cannot receive messages directly.
The MT103 bounces, and the payment has nowhere to go.

Here's how that happens:

→ Beneficiary bank holds a non-connected BIC
→ MT103 and MT202 COV sent to a live BIC
→ Live BIC forwards the funds onward
→ Onward leg uses a normal serial MT103

The assumption was:
"Every BIC can receive a message."

Some banks hold a BIC with the digit 1 in position 8, which marks it as non-connected: it is a SWIFT participant but cannot receive messages directly. The MT103 announcement and the MT202 COV are then sent to a live BIC, which forwards the funds to the non-connected bank over an internal network, usually with a normal serial MT103. The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office forwards payments to subsidiaries and branches.

A BIC with 1 in position 8 is a participant that cannot be reached directly.

BA Takeaway

Route to the live BIC and let it forward the funds. The announcement and the cover go to the live BIC, and the onward leg travels over the internal network, usually as a normal serial MT103.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Non-connected BIC, digit 1 in position 8
→ Live BIC that receives the messages
→ Forwarding over the internal network
→ Serial MT103 for the onward leg

The real requirement isn't "Is the BIC valid?"

It's "What evidence proves which live BIC forwards to this bank?"

Have you ever had a payment bounce because the beneficiary bank's BIC could not receive messages?
takeaway: The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office forwards payments to subsidiaries and branches.

title: The instruction was complete. The payment waited for the currency.
explain:
A customer instructs a EUR 80,000 payment in a foreign currency, with every field complete and every check passed.
The payment does not move.
Hours pass, and the instruction sits untouched, waiting for something the customer never sees.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank receives payment instructions
→ Orders collected until cut-off time
→ Bank checks its nostro balances
→ Buy, sell or do nothing, the decision is made
→ Payment waits for the currency position

The assumption was:
"A complete instruction is executed at once."

A bank does not buy the currency of every payment the moment it is instructed, because it does not know in advance how much foreign currency it will need. It collects orders until a cut-off time and then decides whether to buy, sell or do nothing, based on the balance of orders and the funds already sitting in its nostro accounts. A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete.

A payment can wait for the bank's currency position, even when the instruction is complete.

BA Takeaway

Explain the wait to the customer in terms of the currency position, not the instruction. Orders are collected to cut-off, weighed against nostro balances, and the bank buys, sells or does nothing based on the net position.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Orders collected to cut-off
→ Nostro balances checked
→ Buy, sell or do nothing decision
→ Instruction completeness

The real requirement isn't "Is the instruction complete?"

It's "What evidence proves the currency position is settled and the payment can move?"

Have you ever had to tell a customer the payment was perfect, and still not moving?
takeaway: A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete.

title: French bank, German bank, dollars settled in New York
explain:
A French bank sends USD 500,000 to a German bank.
Two European banks, an American currency, and a payment that never leaves the United States to settle.
The treasurer expects a cross-border journey. Settlement takes one domestic step.

Here's how that happens:

→ French bank instructs its US correspondent
→ Nostro debited in the USA
→ German bank's US correspondent credited
→ Settlement completes in a single domestic step

The assumption was:
"A payment between two European banks settles in Europe."

When a French bank sends USD to a German bank, it tells its US correspondent to debit the nostro and credit the German bank's account with that bank's own US correspondent. Settlement completes in a single domestic step, since both accounts sit in the USA. The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103.

When both accounts sit in the USA, settlement is one domestic step.

BA Takeaway

Find the beneficiary's US correspondent in the Standing Settlement Instructions and state it in the MT103. The nostro is debited, the German bank's account with its own US correspondent is credited, and settlement is done in one domestic step.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sender's US correspondent
→ Nostro debit
→ Beneficiary's US correspondent
→ Standing Settlement Instructions

The real requirement isn't "Which country are the banks in?"

It's "What evidence proves where the settlement accounts sit?"

Have you ever settled a payment between two European banks without the money ever leaving the USA?
takeaway: The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103.

title: The letter of credit is issued. How does the money move?
explain:
A letter of credit for USD 250,000 is issued with an MT700.
The documents are accepted.
Now the beneficiary asks a simple question: how does the money move?
The MT700 does not say.

Here's how that happens:

→ Credit issued with MT700
→ Documents accepted
→ Parties agree the settlement instrument
→ Funds move by serial MT103, or by MT103 plus MT202 COV

The assumption was:
"The MT700 settles the credit."

A letter of credit is issued with an MT700, but the standard does not fix how it must be settled, so the parties agree the payment instrument between themselves. In general the settlement runs through a serial MT103, or through an MT103 together with an MT202 COV. Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted.

The MT700 issues the credit. The MT103 moves the money.

BA Takeaway

Agree the settlement instrument between the parties before the documents are accepted. Either a serial MT103 or an MT103 with an MT202 COV moves the funds, and the agreement is made up front, not after acceptance.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT700, the credit itself
→ Document acceptance
→ Serial MT103 route
→ MT103 plus MT202 COV route

The real requirement isn't "Was the credit issued?"

It's "What evidence proves the parties agreed how the funds will move?"

Have you ever had documents accepted under a credit with no agreed settlement route?
takeaway: Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted.

title: EUR 250,000 from Europe to India, and nobody owned the journey
explain:
A European buyer pays an Indian exporter EUR 250,000.
The payment crosses four legs: a domestic euro rail, a cross-border bridge, an FX conversion and a domestic Indian rail.
Each participant reports only its own leg.
The payment is late, and the chain of calls begins: exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge operator, and nobody can say where the money is.

Here's how that happens:

→ Buyer pays on the domestic euro rail
→ Payment crosses the cross-border bridge
→ Euros convert to rupees
→ Exporter paid on the Indian rail
→ Nobody can say where the money is

The assumption was:
"Each party owns its own leg, so the journey is covered."

With no owner of the end-to-end state, a late payment turns into a chain of calls, exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge operator, and nobody can say where the money is. Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check.

Four legs, four owners, no owner of the journey.

BA Takeaway

Name one owner for the whole corridor. Every leg is mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check, and the owner can say where the money is at any point.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic euro leg
→ Cross-border bridge
→ FX conversion
→ Domestic Indian leg
→ End-to-end owner

The real requirement isn't "Did each leg complete?"

It's "What evidence proves one owner can see the whole journey?"

Have you ever chased a late cross-border payment through four parties, each of whom could only see their own leg?
takeaway: Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check.

title: The payment is visible end to end. Why not the complaint?
explain:
A EUR 55,000 cross-border payment is debited, and the customer can track it end to end across linked payment systems.
Then the payment goes wrong, and the customer raises a complaint.
The complaint cannot travel the same way, and the hardest cross-border problem is back: nobody knows where the payment is.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment debited and tracked end to end
→ Payment goes wrong
→ Complaint raised, but it cannot travel on the linked rails
→ Nobody knows where the payment is

The assumption was:
"Interlinking is only a connectivity project."

Interlinking connects payment systems across countries so a payment can be tracked end to end once it is debited, and the open question is whether the customer-side acceptance of payment instructions can travel the same way, and then complaints and investigations too. If instructions, status and complaints all travel on the interlinked rails, the hardest cross-border problem, not knowing where a payment is, starts to close. That is why interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project.

Interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project.

BA Takeaway

Design interlinking for instructions, status and complaints together. If the complaint travels on the same links as the payment, the question of where the money is finally has an answer.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payment instructions
→ End-to-end tracking
→ Status visibility
→ Complaints and investigations

The real requirement isn't "Are the systems connected?"

It's "What evidence proves a complaint can follow the same path as the payment?"

Have you ever tracked a payment perfectly, then lost it the moment a complaint was raised?
takeaway: That is why interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project.

title: The indirect participant the central bank never sees
explain:
An indirect participant sends EUR 20,000 through its direct participant.
The payment moves, the direct participant's account is debited, and the central bank watches it all happen.
The central bank sees the direct participant, and nobody else.

Here's how that happens:

→ Indirect participant instructs the payment
→ Direct participant sends the debit
→ Central bank sees only the direct participant

The assumption was:
"The central bank watches every participant."

From the central bank standpoint the risk is liquidity: whether the indirect participant can meet its financial obligations. Ensuring that funding is normally the direct participant business, since the direct participant must confirm the indirect participant holds enough before sending debit payments. The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than dealing with the indirect participant.

The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant.

BA Takeaway

Put the funding check on the direct participant. It must confirm the indirect participant holds enough before sending debit payments, because the central bank oversees the direct participant as a whole and never deals with the indirect participant directly.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Liquidity risk
→ Direct participant confirms funding
→ Central bank sees the direct participant
→ Oversight covers the direct participant whole

The real requirement isn't "Can the indirect participant pay?"

It's "What evidence proves the direct participant confirmed the funding before sending?"

Have you ever assumed the central bank was watching a participant it never sees?
takeaway: The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than dealing with the indirect participant.

title: EUR 20,000 returned because the requirement quoted the rulebook
explain:
A EUR 20,000 payment is returned by the beneficiary bank.
The developers say they built exactly what the requirement said.
The requirement quoted the scheme rulebook, word for word.

Here's how that happens:

→ Scheme rule copied into the requirement as written
→ Developers build the rule literally
→ The payment is rejected at the beneficiary bank
→ Nobody can say what the system was supposed to do instead

The assumption was:
"Copying the rule into the requirement is the same as specifying it."

Why?

Payment scheme rules are written in technical language, but developers and business users need them as a clear trigger, decision, rule, timeline and system behaviour. Translating a rule into what happens, when, and what the system must do is what makes it buildable.

A quoted rule ≠ A buildable requirement.

Jargon left in a requirement produces a system that does the wrong thing confidently, so plain, precise wording is a quality control, not a courtesy.

BA Takeaway

Translate every scheme rule into trigger, decision, rule, timeline and system behaviour.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Trigger that starts the rule
→ Decision the system must make
→ Rule it must apply
→ Timeline it must meet
→ Behaviour the user must see

The real requirement isn't "Did we quote the rule?"

It's "What evidence proves a developer could build the right behaviour from this wording alone?"

Have you seen a system do the wrong thing confidently because the requirement was quoted, not translated?
takeaway: Jargon left in a requirement produces a system that does the wrong thing confidently, so plain, precise wording is a quality control, not a courtesy.

title: The EUR 1 million project that stalled on one unasked question
explain:
A EUR 1 million payments project stalls in its third month.
Compliance says the requirement was never theirs.
Developers say the requirement was never buildable.
The BA says everyone agreed it in the workshop.

Here's how that happens:

→ Stakeholders from compliance, business, developers and vendors meet
→ The BA presents the payment flow and everyone nods
→ Nobody is asked whether they understand the concepts or the sequence
→ Three months later, each team is building a different payment

The assumption was:
"A nod in the workshop means the stakeholder understood."

Why?

A payments BA works with many stakeholders at once, across several projects and dependent systems. The work starts by asking whether each stakeholder understands the payment concepts, the sequence of payments, the business and its rules, and the payment journey, and whether the BA understands the system, the processing and where they fit in the flow. When a stakeholder does not know an answer, the BA helps them understand the question and reach it.

A nod ≠ Understanding.

Asking the right questions is the core of stakeholder management, not a soft skill on the side.

BA Takeaway

Test understanding with questions, never with nods.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Concepts the stakeholder understands
→ Sequence and journey they can describe
→ Rules they can apply
→ The BA's own understanding of the system

The real requirement isn't "Did everyone agree in the workshop?"

It's "What evidence proves each stakeholder could explain the payment flow back to you?"

Have you seen a project stall because a nod was mistaken for understanding?
takeaway: When a stakeholder does not know an answer, the BA helps them understand the question and reach it, because that translation is what makes the requirements workable, and asking the right questions is the core of stakeholder management, not a soft skill on the side.

title: The EUR 500,000 release nobody validated in production
explain:
A EUR 500,000 payments change goes live on a Friday.
By Monday, adoption is near zero and two defects are open.
Nobody can say whether the change delivered what was promised.

Here's how that happens:

→ Discovery finds the business problem and the real users
→ Analysis turns it into testable requirements
→ Build and test keep the increment honest against scope
→ Release ships, and the analyst moves to the next project

The assumption was:
"Release is the end of the analyst's job."

Why?

The analyst owns the thread from discovery to live running. After release the work is not over: the analyst validates the outcome in production and reports what remains open. A lifecycle without that closing loop leaves value unproven.

Shipped ≠ Delivered.

A lifecycle without the closing loop leaves value unproven.

BA Takeaway

Own the thread from discovery to validated live outcome.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Discovery of the real problem and users
→ Requirements that can be tested
→ Build kept honest against scope
→ Post-release validation in production

The real requirement isn't "Did we release on Friday?"

It's "What evidence proves the change works in production and the open items are reported?"

Have you seen a release declared done while nobody checked whether it worked live?
takeaway: A lifecycle without that closing loop leaves value unproven.

title: The EUR 200,000 sprint that failed at review
explain:
A EUR 200,000 payments sprint reaches review.
The increment fails its acceptance criteria.
The analyst says the criteria were never clear. The team says the analyst was never there.

Here's how that happens:

→ Refinement skips the analyst, stories stay vague
→ Planning sets scope the team cannot deliver
→ Delivery runs with questions unanswered
→ Review tests the increment against criteria nobody agreed

The assumption was:
"The analyst's job starts at review."

Why?

In Scrum the analyst works the sprint, not around it: refinement turns vague stories into clear acceptance criteria, planning grounds scope and priority in what the team can actually deliver, and delivery is a running conversation as detail emerges. Review and acceptance close the loop by testing the built increment against the criteria agreed.

An analyst who only appears at review is too late to shape anything.

Present at review ≠ Present in the sprint.

BA Takeaway

Work the sprint, not around it, from refinement to acceptance.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Refinement into clear acceptance criteria
→ Planning grounded in what can be delivered
→ Delivery as a running conversation
→ Review against the agreed criteria

The real requirement isn't "Did we hold a review?"

It's "What evidence proves the criteria were agreed in refinement and tested at review?"

Have you seen a sprint fail at review because the analyst only arrived at the end?
takeaway: An analyst who only appears at review is too late to shape anything.

title: The EUR 50,000 payment that was correct, and three seconds too slow
explain:
A EUR 50,000 payment is validated correctly and posted to the right ledger.
The customer abandons it anyway.
The payment took three seconds longer than the channel allows, and the session timed out.

Here's how that happens:

→ Functional requirement: validate the payment, post the ledger entry
→ The system does both, correctly
→ No non-functional requirement was ever written for response time
→ The customer session times out before the confirmation arrives

The assumption was:
"If the payment is correct, it works."

Why?

Functional requirements state what the system must do, such as validating a payment or posting a ledger entry, while non-functional requirements state how well it must do it: performance, security, availability, usability and supportability. Both belong in the specification as explicit, testable statements.

Correct ≠ Usable.

A payment that is correct yet too slow or unavailable still fails the customer. Function without fitness for use is not a working payment.

BA Takeaway

Write both kinds of requirement as explicit, testable statements.

Keep these controls separate:

→ What the system must do
→ How fast it must do it
→ How available and secure it must be
→ How usable it must be under load

The real requirement isn't "Does the payment validate?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment is correct, fast enough and available when the customer needs it?"

Have you seen a correct payment fail because nobody specified how well it had to perform?
takeaway: Function without fitness for use is not a working payment.

title: The EUR 100,000 refund story that hid the exception path
explain:
A team writes a user story for a EUR 100,000 refund.
It says what the user wants and why.
In testing, the refund fails on a duplicate payment, and nobody wrote down what should happen.

Here's how that happens:

→ User story written: outcome led, what the user wants and why
→ The story is used for prioritisation and conversation
→ The exception path is never described
→ Testing finds the duplicate case, and the team guesses

The assumption was:
"One form fits every need."

Why?

A user story is outcome led: it states what a user wants to achieve and why, which makes it the right tool for prioritisation and conversation. A use case is interaction led: it pins down steps, actors and outcomes for one interaction, including decisions and exception paths. Choose by the need in front of you, not by team habit.

The wrong form hides the detail that matters.

A story for outcomes ≠ A use case for interaction.

BA Takeaway

Choose the form by the need in front of you, not by team habit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Outcome the user wants, and why
→ Steps, actors and outcomes of the interaction
→ Decisions along the way
→ Exception paths when things go wrong

The real requirement isn't "Did we write a story?"

It's "What evidence proves the form we chose captures the detail this need actually has?"

Have you seen a defect hide in a detail the chosen form never asked for?
takeaway: The wrong form hides the detail that matters.

title: The EUR 300,000 BRD the developers could not build from
explain:
A EUR 300,000 payments change has a thick BRD.
The developers say it tells them nothing they can build.
The business says it already approved the requirements.

Here's how that happens:

→ Business requirements document states what the business needs and why
→ The document goes to developers as the build instruction
→ Developers ask for the detail: fields, rules, behaviour
→ The business points at the BRD and says it is already approved

The assumption was:
"One document serves every reader."

Why?

The business requirements document states what the business needs and why, the functional requirements document states in detail what the system must do, and a use case describes one specific interaction between actors and the system. Selection turns on audience, complexity, traceability and delivery context, so each reader gets the detail they need and nothing they do not.

Approved ≠ Buildable.

The right artefact is the one its reader can act on.

BA Takeaway

Match the artefact to its reader, every time.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Business need and why (BRD)
→ What the system must do in detail (FRD)
→ One interaction between actors and system (use case)
→ The reader who must act on it

The real requirement isn't "Did we write a requirements document?"

It's "What evidence proves the reader of this document can act on it without asking for another one?"

Have you seen a project stall because the right document went to the wrong reader?
takeaway: The right artefact is the one its reader can act on.

title: The EUR 1 million release report that hid the open risks
explain:
A EUR 1 million payments release goes live.
The first stakeholder report shows green across the board.
A week later, adoption is 12 percent and three critical defects are open.

Here's how that happens:

→ Report covers adoption, incidents, defects, service levels, benefits and risks
→ The report writer leaves out the open risks to keep it tidy
→ Stakeholders read green and move on
→ The defects surface in production, and nobody is prepared

The assumption was:
"A tidy report is a good report."

Why?

After release, stakeholders need one factual, regular report covering adoption, incidents, defects, service levels, benefits realised and open risks. Adoption shows whether the change is used, incidents and defects show what is still broken, service levels show whether it performs, and benefits and open risks show whether the intended outcome is on track. A report built this way lets stakeholders decide what needs attention next.

Green everywhere ≠ Everything fine.

Reporting that hides the open items is worse than no report at all.

BA Takeaway

Report the open items first, not last, and never leave them out.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Adoption, whether the change is used
→ Incidents and defects, what is still broken
→ Service levels, whether it performs
→ Benefits realised and open risks

The real requirement isn't "Did we send a report?"

It's "What evidence proves the report showed every open risk, not just the green ones?"

Have you seen a green report hide a release that was failing?
takeaway: Reporting that hides the open items is worse than no report at all.

title: The EUR 400,000 upgrade deferred because it was sold as features
explain:
A team asks for EUR 400,000 to upgrade the payments platform.
The business case lists features: new messages, new screens, new APIs.
The steering committee defers it. Again.

Here's how that happens:

→ Case presented in technical detail: features, messages, screens
→ Stakeholders ask what it delivers for customers and revenue
→ The case has no answer in their terms
→ The decision is deferred to the next quarter

The assumption was:
"Good features sell themselves."

Why?

Stakeholders decide on outcomes, not on technical detail, so present the change in their terms: the outcome it delivers, the customer impact, the revenue or cost effect, the compliance position, the timing and the decisions needed. Keep the language plain and tie every point to something the stakeholder is accountable for.

A case argued on features gets deferred.

A case argued on value gets decided.

BA Takeaway

Argue every change on value, in the stakeholder's own terms.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Outcome the change delivers
→ Customer impact
→ Revenue or cost effect
→ Compliance position, timing and decisions needed

The real requirement isn't "Did we list the features?"

It's "What evidence proves the stakeholder could see their own outcome in this case?"

Have you seen a good change deferred because it was sold as features, not value?
takeaway: A case argued on value gets decided; a case argued on features gets deferred.

title: The EUR 50,000 payments outage customers heard about from Twitter
explain:
A payments outage blocks EUR 50,000 of customer payments.
Support has no status to give.
Customers learn about the outage from social media before the bank tells them.

Here's how that happens:

→ Outage starts, payments stop
→ Support is asked for a status and has nothing repeatable
→ No update is promised, so no update is given
→ Customers assume the worst and call in a flood

The assumption was:
"No news is fine until we have a fix."

Why?

During an incident, support needs a status it can repeat to customers without guessing: the symptom in plain language, the users affected, a workaround if one exists, the owner, the severity and the time of the next update. Update at the promised time even if nothing has changed, because silence makes customers assume the worst.

Silence ≠ Reassurance.

Reliable updates are part of the fix, not an extra.

BA Takeaway

Give support a repeatable status, and update at the promised time even with no change.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Symptom in plain language
→ Users affected and workaround
→ Owner and severity
→ Time of the next update, kept even with no news

The real requirement isn't "Did we fix it fast?"

It's "What evidence proves customers were told, on time, in words support could repeat?"

Have you seen an incident made worse by silence while the fix was already under way?
takeaway: Reliable updates are part of the fix, not an extra.

title: The EUR 250,000 scope dispute nobody wrote down
explain:
A EUR 250,000 payments project ends in a scope dispute.
The vendor says the extra work was agreed in a meeting.
The business says it never approved it.
There is no record either way.

Here's how that happens:

→ Meeting agrees an extra scope item, verbally
→ No one writes down the action, the owner or the due date
→ The decision and its assumptions are never recorded
→ Approval is inferred from silence, and the dispute begins

The assumption was:
"Everyone was in the room, so everyone agreed."

Why?

Written communication is the record that protects a delivery: meeting notes name the action, the owner and the due date, decisions are recorded with the assumptions behind them, and approval is obtained explicitly rather than inferred from silence. A sign-off only works if it states exactly what was approved and by whom.

Silence ≠ Approval.

If it is not written down, it was not agreed.

BA Takeaway

Write the action, the owner, the due date, the decision and the approval, every time.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Meeting notes with action, owner and due date
→ Decisions recorded with their assumptions
→ Approval obtained explicitly
→ Sign-off stating exactly what was approved and by whom

The real requirement isn't "Were we all in the meeting?"

It's "What evidence proves this was agreed, by whom, and on what assumptions?"

Have you seen a scope dispute where the only record was everyone's memory?
takeaway: If it is not written down, it was not agreed.

title: The operations analyst whose EUR 30,000 salary pitch listed only a job title
explain:
An operations analyst applies for a business analyst role paying EUR 30,000 more.
The CV lists the old job title and the old employer.
The recruiter cannot see a single BA skill in it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Years in operations, support and product work
→ CV lists the job title and hopes the reader connects the dots
→ Recruiter searches for elicitation, documentation and delivery support
→ The profile never surfaces for the role

The assumption was:
"The job title speaks for itself."

Why?

Moving into business analysis from another domain works when transferable skills are mapped to the work an analyst actually does: experience in operations, support or product maps to domain knowledge, elicitation, documentation, delivery support and outcome measurement. State the mapping explicitly, with concrete examples of work done, rather than listing a previous job title and hoping the reader makes the connection.

A mapped skill is a hiring argument; an unmapped job title is just a label.

BA Takeaway

Map every transferable skill to BA work, with a concrete example attached.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domain knowledge from prior work
→ Elicitation and documentation shown by example
→ Delivery support and outcome measurement
→ The job title, which proves nothing alone

The real requirement isn't "Did we list the old job?"

It's "What evidence proves this experience is BA work, in the recruiter's own words?"

Have you seen a strong candidate invisible because their CV listed titles, not mapped skills?

title: Six months learning tools, and still no interview for a payments BA role
explain:
A career changer spends six months learning BA tools.
The profile lists every tool on the market.
No recruiter calls for a payments BA role.

Here's how that happens:

→ Tools learned first, domain chosen never
→ Profile shows tool skill, no domain understanding
→ Recruiter searches for payments domain credibility
→ The profile reads as a tool user, not a payments analyst

The assumption was:
"Tools are what get the interview."

Why?

Before learning tools, choose the domain to work in, weighing transferable experience, demand for the domain, genuine interest and a realistic entry path. An analyst is hired for domain understanding first and tool skill second, so a focused domain choice makes learning faster and a profile credible to a recruiter in that domain.

Tools are easy to learn; credibility in a domain is what gets the interview.

Tool skill ≠ Domain credibility.

BA Takeaway

Pick the domain first, then learn the tools it actually uses.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Transferable experience into the domain
→ Demand for the domain
→ Genuine interest in it
→ A realistic entry path

The real requirement isn't "How many tools do we know?"

It's "What evidence proves we understand the domain a recruiter is hiring for?"

takeaway: Tools are easy to learn; credibility in a domain is what gets the interview.

title: The EUR 60,000 BA role that never found a perfect candidate
explain:
A recruiter fills a EUR 60,000 business analyst role.
The perfect candidate exists, with the exact domain and skills.
The recruiter never finds them, because their profile uses none of the role's words.

Here's how that happens:

→ Recruiter searches by keywords that match the role
→ The candidate's profile uses different words for the same work
→ The search never surfaces the profile
→ The role goes to a weaker candidate who used the right keywords

The assumption was:
"Good work speaks for itself."

Why?

Recruiters search by keywords that match the role they are filling, so align profile keywords with the target role, the domain, the skills and the verifiable experience, and a search for that role will surface the profile. Claim only what can be evidenced, because a keyword that cannot be backed up damages credibility in the first conversation.

Visibility gets the call; evidence wins it.

Invisible ≠ Unqualified.

BA Takeaway

Align keywords with the role, and back every one with evidence.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Target role keywords
→ Domain keywords
→ Skills keywords
→ Verifiable experience behind each claim

The real requirement isn't "Are we good at the work?"

It's "What evidence proves the recruiter can find us, and that every keyword survives the first conversation?"

title: The EUR 80,000 interview lost on one confident wrong answer
explain:
A candidate interviews for an EUR 80,000 payments BA role.
One question is outside their knowledge.
They answer confidently, and wrongly. The interview ends there.

Here's how that happens:

→ Interviewer asks about a payment flow the candidate has not worked on
→ The candidate guesses rather than saying so
→ The reasoning sounds confident and falls apart on the follow-up
→ The panel marks down judgement, not just knowledge

The assumption was:
"Never admit you do not know."

Why?

In an interview, not knowing an answer is acceptable if it is handled honestly: state the assumptions being made, explain the reasoning that follows from them, and identify what would need to be validated before committing to an answer. Never bluff. Interviewers test judgement and honesty as much as knowledge, and a confident guess that turns out wrong is worse than a clear statement of what is known and what is not.

A confident guess ≠ A good answer.

BA Takeaway

Say what you assume, show your reasoning, and name what must be validated.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Assumptions being made, stated plainly
→ Reasoning that follows from them
→ What must be validated before committing
→ What is known, and what is not

The real requirement isn't "Did we answer every question?"

It's "What evidence proves our judgement is sound even when our knowledge runs out?"

Have you seen a confident wrong answer cost more than an honest 'I don't know'?

title: The unfamiliar EUR 45,000 scenario that rewarded method, not memory
explain:
A candidate faces an unfamiliar EUR 45,000 payments scenario in an interview.
They have never seen this flow before.
They answer in a fixed order, and the panel hires them.

Here's how that happens:

→ Scenario presented: a payment flow the candidate does not know
→ The candidate clarifies the assumptions first
→ The flow is broken into stages, risks named at each one
→ The candidate states what evidence they would get before deciding

The assumption was:
"You need to know the answer to answer well."

Why?

Face an unfamiliar scenario in a fixed order: clarify the assumptions, break the flow into its stages, identify the risks at each stage, and state what evidence would be obtained before deciding. This structure shows clear thinking even when the domain is new, and it prevents the answer from becoming a guess.

Method is what carries you when knowledge runs out.

A guess ≠ An answer.

BA Takeaway

Run every unfamiliar scenario through the same fixed order.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Assumptions clarified first
→ Flow broken into stages
→ Risks identified at each stage
→ Evidence needed before deciding

The real requirement isn't "Did we know this scenario?"

It's "What evidence proves we thought clearly even where our knowledge ran out?"

Have you seen a candidate win on method when memory had nothing to offer?
